analysis.one_liner: Gives Medicare beneficiaries a card to buy prescription drugs at the discounted prices the federal government already pays.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote: it died in committee at the end of the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given every Medicare beneficiary a drug benefit card letting them buy prescriptions at the same discounted prices the federal government gets through the Federal Supply Schedule — prices the bill's findings say are on average half what seniors pay at the counter, and in some cases one-fifteenth as much. Pharmacies could volunteer to participate and buy drugs at that federal price plus a small administrative fee. The bill was referred to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — roughly the 39 million older and disabled Americans then on Medicare — who pay cash at the pharmacy and currently pay about twice what the government's most favored customers pay for the same drugs. The bill's own findings say more than one in eight older Americans sometimes choose between food and medicine, and estimate the card would cut their drug prices by more than 40%. Participating pharmacies would gain a reliable stream of card-holding customers with a preserved dispensing margin.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare beneficiary would receive a drug benefit card letting them buy covered outpatient drugs from participating pharmacies at reduced prices.

The discount is pegged to the Federal Supply Schedule price that federal agencies — the VA, Medicaid-adjacent programs, and others — already pay, which the bill's findings say is on average half the price seniors pay, and in some cases one-fifteenth as much.

The bill's findings estimate the policy would cut prescription prices for Medicare beneficiaries by more than 40 percent, and note that over one in eight older Americans report choosing between food and medicine.
Pharmacies would buy the drugs at the federal schedule price plus a modest administrative-cost add-on, so dispensing pharmacies keep their role and margin rather than being displaced.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would have to sell to participating pharmacies at the low federal schedule price instead of the much higher cash price seniors pay. The bill's findings tie the industry's roughly $20 billion in annual profits to this two-tier pricing, so ending the premium paid by seniors comes directly out of manufacturer revenue. No cost falls on the federal treasury; the program is administered through existing drug distribution channels.

drawbacks.text: This is a discount card, not a drug benefit: seniors would still pay the full discounted price out of pocket, with no coverage for catastrophic drug costs — someone with expensive chronic prescriptions would still face large bills.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would set the discount price administratively, and drug manufacturers argued then, as they argue against similar proposals now, that government-set prices below market levels reduce revenue available for research into new medicines.
Pharmacy participation is voluntary, so the card's usefulness would depend on enough drugstores signing up in any given area.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors who pay cash for prescriptions, the upside was large and immediate — the same pills at roughly the price the VA pays — while the cost was borne entirely by manufacturers' pricing power, not by taxpayers. The real design weakness is that it stops short of an insurance benefit, leaving seniors exposed to high drug costs even after the discount. Even so, it was a serious, targeted answer to a documented two-tier pricing problem, and it never got the chance to be debated or amended.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late September 1998, it was sent to the Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to a Commerce subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 — no hearing, no markup, no vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen introduced the bill on September 25, 1998, with 27 original cosponsors joining at introduction.

It was referred to both the House Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction — a double referral that requires two committees to act before a bill can reach the floor.
On September 30, 1998, it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment, its last recorded action.
The bill accumulated 53 cosponsors — 52 Democrats and one Independent — but the Congress adjourned on January 3, 1999 without the bill ever being reported out of committee or brought to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept selling to cash-paying seniors at retail prices while federal programs paid far less, with no mechanism created to close that gap. The gap was not addressed by law until the Medicare drug benefit enacted in 2003. Seniors kept paying the higher prices for another five years.

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Allen
for.role: U.S. Representative, Maine (2nd district); bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness for Seniors Act and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 52 of 206 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior members such as Henry Waxman, John Dingell-era committee members, Pete Stark, and Bernie Sanders (I) as the sole Independent cosponsor.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor; the bill's only movement was a referral to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment four days after introduction.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending federal discounted prices to Medicare beneficiaries, lobbying against Medicare drug price legislation during this period as the industry's profits depended on the two-tier pricing the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to charge cash-paying seniors roughly double — and in extreme cases many times — what their favored institutional customers pay, directly cutting into the roughly $20 billion in annual profits the bill's findings attribute to this price discrimination. Their gain from the bill dying was seniors continuing to pay retail prices.

Participating pharmacies would get a guaranteed new customer base of Medicare card-holders buying at a price set to preserve their dispensing margin, with purchase volume capped at what they actually sell to card-holders. Their existing role as the channel for prescriptions is locked in rather than displaced.

Insurers already received the favored-customer pricing the bill extends to seniors, so the bill narrows their relative price advantage without taking it away. Their benefit over cash-paying seniors shrinks slightly but their contracted prices are untouched.
